questions.question: Kubernetes vs Docker Swarm vs HashiCorp Nomad — which orchestrator and when?
questions.title: Kubernetes vs Docker Swarm vs Nomad: Container Orchestration Compared
questions.direct_answer: Kubernetes wins for production at any meaningful scale — the de facto standard, massive ecosystem, every cloud provides managed K8s (EKS/GKE/AKS), every tool integrates. Docker Swarm wins for very small teams who want Docker-Compose-style simplicity at low scale — but is effectively in maintenance mode and shouldn't be picked for new projects. Nomad wins for mixed workloads (containers + VMs + Java JARs + raw binaries) and teams already invested in HashiCorp stack (Consul, Vault) — simpler than K8s, but smaller ecosystem.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of orchestration landscape and pragmatic tool selection
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Picking Kubernetes for a 3-service hobby project without acknowledging the operational complexity it brings; or recommending Swarm in 2026 when it's effectively dead
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the operational burden curve, the K8s ecosystem moat, Nomad's niche for mixed workloads, and managed K8s as the right answer for most teams

sections.title: One Tool Won, Two Survive in Niches
sections.content:
Container orchestration in 2026 is effectively a one-horse race: **Kubernetes won.** Every major cloud provides managed K8s (EKS, GKE, AKS), every observability/CI/security tool integrates with K8s first, and the talent pool is built around K8s primitives. The question isn't usually "K8s or alternative" — it's "managed K8s or roll your own?"

That said, two alternatives survive in legitimate niches:

**Docker Swarm** is Docker's built-in orchestrator: dead simple to set up (`docker swarm init`), Compose-file-compatible deployments, single binary. It was the simpler-than-K8s option in 2016–2018; today it's effectively in maintenance mode — Docker Inc.'s focus shifted to developer experience (Docker Desktop, Compose) and away from orchestration. Don't pick Swarm for new production work; the ecosystem and roadmap aren't there.

**HashiCorp Nomad** is the genuine alternative for specific cases: it orchestrates containers AND VMs AND raw binaries AND Java JARs in one scheduler. Simpler architecture than K8s (one binary for client + server, no complex API resource model). Wins when you need to schedule heterogeneous workloads (mix of containers and legacy services), or when you're already invested in Consul/Vault and want consistent operational patterns. Smaller ecosystem than K8s but very mature.

The pragmatic 2026 default: **managed Kubernetes** (EKS, GKE, AKS) for any production workload past about 5 services. Below that scale, container orchestration may be over-engineering — docker-compose on a single VM or serverless (Lambda, Cloud Run) often wins.

sections.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Kubernetes | Docker Swarm | Nomad |
|--------|------------|--------------|-------|
| **Setup complexity** | High (or pay for managed) | Very low (`docker swarm init`) | Low (one binary) |
| **Workload types** | Containers (+ VMs via KubeVirt) | Containers only | Containers + VMs + JARs + raw exec |
| **Service discovery** | Built-in (kube-dns) | Built-in (DNS-based) | Via Consul (separate but integrated) |
| **Networking** | CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, etc.) | Built-in overlay | CNI or host networking |
| **Storage** | CSI plugins (50+) | Volumes (limited) | CSI plugins |
| **Configuration** | YAML (verbose), Helm, Kustomize | docker-compose.yml | HCL (Terraform-style) |
| **Ecosystem** | Massive (CNCF graduated, 1000+ projects) | Tiny | Medium (HashiCorp + 3rd party) |
| **Cloud-managed** | EKS, GKE, AKS, all major clouds | None | HCP Nomad (HashiCorp managed) |
| **Talent pool** | Huge | Small, shrinking | Small but specialized |
| **Roadmap** | Active (quarterly releases) | Effectively stalled | Active (HashiCorp) |
| **Best for** | Production at scale; default for most | Tiny teams, low scale (legacy) | Mixed workloads; HashiCorp shops |
| **Companies** | Google, Spotify, Airbnb, Netflix, every FAANG | Some legacy small shops | Cloudflare, Roblox, Trivago, Pandora |
| **Operational burden** | High (or buy managed) | Low | Medium |

sections.title: Decision Tree: Which Orchestrator (or None)
sections.content:
**Pick managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) when:**
- You're running 5+ services in production
- You want the broadest ecosystem (every tool you'll need has a K8s integration)
- You can pay for managed (control plane is operationally hard; let the cloud run it)
- Your team has K8s skills or budget to acquire them
- Long-term bet on cloud-native ecosystem (service mesh, GitOps, autoscaling)
- The vast majority of new production deployments

**Pick self-hosted Kubernetes when:**
- Air-gapped environment (regulated, government) where managed K8s isn't an option
- Need extensive customization the managed offerings don't support
- Strong existing on-prem infrastructure team with K8s expertise
- Cost optimization at very large scale (managed control planes get expensive at huge scale)

**Pick Nomad when:**
- You schedule mixed workloads — containers PLUS legacy VMs PLUS Java JARs PLUS raw binaries; K8s can do this with KubeVirt but Nomad does it natively
- You're invested in HashiCorp stack (Consul service mesh, Vault for secrets, Terraform for infra) and want consistent ops
- You want simpler than K8s but more capable than Swarm; one Nomad binary vs K8s's many components
- Examples: Cloudflare runs Nomad at huge scale for heterogeneous workloads; Trivago runs both K8s and Nomad for different use cases

**Pick Docker Swarm when:**
- You have an existing Swarm deployment and migration cost is too high; otherwise no
- Don't pick for new projects; the ecosystem and roadmap are not there

**Skip orchestration entirely when:**
- 1–3 services and small scale: docker-compose on a single VM, or serverless (AWS Lambda, Cloud Run, Container Apps) is simpler
- Pure FaaS workloads: Lambda + DynamoDB + API Gateway has no orchestration overhead
- Single-tenant SaaS with one production environment: managed services beat K8s for ops-burden-vs-features

**Anti-pattern**: adopting Kubernetes "because everyone does" for a 3-service startup. The operational complexity — ingress, networking, RBAC, observability, upgrades — is significant; you may spend more time managing K8s than building product. Stay on managed services (App Runner, Cloud Run, ECS Fargate) until scale or feature needs justify K8s.

sections.title: Hidden Trade-offs and Common Mistakes
sections.content:
**The K8s ecosystem is the moat.** It's not that K8s is technically the best orchestrator — it's that every tool you need (observability, GitOps, service mesh, secret management, security scanning) integrates with K8s first and foremost. Choosing anything else means re-implementing or going without these integrations.

**Managed K8s is not zero-ops.** EKS, GKE, AKS run the control plane for you, but you still own: node fleet sizing, cluster upgrades, ingress, networking, RBAC policies, observability stack, cost management, and the hundred Helm charts you'll deploy. Budget for a platform team.

**Swarm's death is real.** Docker Inc. hasn't shipped meaningful Swarm features in years; CVEs get patched but the orchestrator hasn't evolved. Teams on Swarm are increasingly stuck — talent dries up, ecosystem doesn't add features, migration to K8s becomes inevitable. Plan for migration if you're on Swarm.

**Nomad's tradeoff: smaller ecosystem.** You can run Nomad simply, but when you need a service mesh, you pull in Consul. When you need secrets, you pull in Vault. The HashiCorp stack is excellent but separate — not bundled like K8s. For heterogeneous workloads this is a feature; for pure container workloads it's friction K8s doesn't have.

**Multi-cluster K8s is hard.** Running K8s in 5 regions across 3 clouds requires tooling (Karmada, Submariner, Cluster API). Nomad handles multi-region more simply via federation. If true multi-region is core, evaluate Nomad.

**Cost at scale.** EKS charges $0.10/hr per cluster; managed K8s gets expensive at 100+ clusters. Self-hosted at huge scale or Nomad (no per-cluster fee) become more attractive.

**Don't underestimate the talent gap.** K8s expertise is expensive but available. Nomad expertise is rarer; you'll train your team. Swarm expertise is increasingly hard to find.

**Serverless undercuts orchestration entirely.** AWS Lambda, Cloud Run, Container Apps eliminate the orchestration layer for many workloads. "Containers but managed" is now a real option (Fargate, Cloud Run); for stateless HTTP services, this is often the right answer over any orchestrator.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Kubernetes won** — it's the de facto standard; every cloud provides managed offerings (EKS, GKE, AKS); every tool integrates with K8s first
- **Managed K8s is the default for production at scale** — don't run your own control plane unless you must; let the cloud handle that operational burden
- **Docker Swarm is effectively dead** — don't pick for new projects; plan migration if you're on it
- **Nomad has a real niche** — mixed workloads (containers + VMs + JARs), HashiCorp shops, simpler ops than K8s; smaller ecosystem is the trade-off
- **Skip orchestration when you can** — 1–3 services on docker-compose or serverless (Lambda, Cloud Run, Fargate) is simpler than any orchestrator
- **K8s isn't zero-ops even managed** — you own ingress, RBAC, observability, upgrades, and 100 Helm charts; budget for a platform team

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Container orchestration in 2026 is effectively a one-horse race — Kubernetes won. The interesting question isn't usually "K8s or alternative," it's "managed K8s or roll your own," or sometimes "K8s or skip orchestration entirely."

**Kubernetes — the de facto standard**
- Every major cloud provides managed K8s: EKS on AWS, GKE on Google, AKS on Azure
- Every tool you'll need has a K8s-first integration: observability (Prometheus, Datadog), GitOps (ArgoCD, Flux), service mesh (Istio, Linkerd), security scanning, autoscaling
- The ecosystem is the moat — it's not that K8s is technically the best orchestrator, it's that everything else integrates with it first
- The default for production at any meaningful scale (5+ services)

**Docker Swarm — effectively in maintenance mode**
- Was the simpler-than-K8s option in 2016–2018; today Docker Inc.'s focus is on developer experience (Desktop, Compose), not orchestration
- Don't pick for new production work; the roadmap and ecosystem aren't there
- Plan migration if you're on it; talent pool shrinks year over year

**Nomad — real niche for mixed workloads**
- HashiCorp's orchestrator; one binary for server + client; simpler architecture than K8s
- Killer feature: schedules containers AND VMs AND raw binaries AND Java JARs in one scheduler; K8s can do this with KubeVirt but Nomad does it natively
- Wins for HashiCorp shops invested in Consul service mesh and Vault for secrets; consistent operational patterns across the stack
- Examples: Cloudflare runs Nomad at huge scale for heterogeneous workloads; Trivago and Roblox use it
- Trade-off: smaller ecosystem than K8s; you compose Consul, Vault, and other tools rather than getting them bundled

**The decision tree**
- Production at scale, want broadest ecosystem: managed Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS) — the right answer for most teams
- Air-gapped or extensive customization needs: self-hosted K8s
- Mixed workloads (containers + VMs + legacy services), HashiCorp stack: Nomad
- Existing Swarm only: don't pick new, plan migration
- Tiny scale (1–3 services): skip orchestration — docker-compose on a VM or serverless (Lambda, Cloud Run, Fargate) is simpler

**The traps to call out**
- Adopting K8s for a 3-service startup is over-engineering — the operational complexity (ingress, RBAC, networking, observability, upgrades) is significant; stay on managed services until scale justifies K8s
- Managed K8s is not zero-ops — the cloud runs the control plane but you own everything else; budget for a platform team
- Multi-cluster K8s is hard — Karmada, Submariner, Cluster API for federation; Nomad handles multi-region more simply
- Cost at huge scale — EKS at $0.10/hr per cluster gets expensive at 100+ clusters; self-hosted or Nomad become more attractive

**The serverless undercut**
- Lambda, Cloud Run, Container Apps eliminate the orchestration layer entirely for many workloads
- For stateless HTTP services, "containers but managed" is often the right answer over any orchestrator
- The orchestration question is now: do I need orchestration at all, or do my workloads fit serverless?

**Default recommendation**
- New SaaS startup: serverless (Lambda or Cloud Run) until scale or feature needs push you to K8s
- Mid-size production: managed K8s (EKS/GKE/AKS); pay for the control plane
- Large enterprise with HashiCorp investment: Nomad is a serious option
- Air-gapped or regulated: self-hosted K8s with a dedicated platform team

questions.question: Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet vs Job — which Kubernetes workload and when?
questions.title: K8s Workload Types Compared: Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job
questions.direct_answer: **Deployment** for stateless services (web APIs, microservices) — pods are interchangeable; rolling updates; the default 90% of the time. **StatefulSet** for stateful services with stable identity (databases, Kafka, ZooKeeper) — pods get stable names (pod-0, pod-1) and persistent volumes that survive rescheduling. **DaemonSet** for one-pod-per-node (log collectors, monitoring agents, CSI drivers, kube-proxy). **Job/CronJob** for run-to-completion or scheduled tasks (batch processing, backups, migrations).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of K8s workload primitives and when each fits
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using StatefulSet 'because we have state' when the state is in an external database; Deployment is correct in that case
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss why StatefulSets are slower (ordered rollouts), the role of headless services for StatefulSets, and the operational pain of DaemonSets at scale

sections.title: Four Workload Primitives for Four Different Patterns
sections.content:
Kubernetes workloads are not interchangeable — each is purpose-built for a specific operational pattern. Picking the wrong one leads to subtle pain.

**Deployment** is for stateless workloads where pods are interchangeable. Web servers, microservices, anything that scales horizontally and doesn't care which replica handles a request. Deployments manage ReplicaSets which manage Pods; rolling updates are the default; rollback via `kubectl rollout undo`. The 90% case for application workloads.

**StatefulSet** is for workloads that need stable network identity and persistent storage. Pod names are deterministic (`mysql-0`, `mysql-1`, `mysql-2`) and stable across restarts. Each pod gets its own PersistentVolumeClaim that follows it through rescheduling. Used for databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL), distributed systems (Kafka, ZooKeeper, Cassandra, Elasticsearch). Slower rollouts — pods come up one at a time in order to preserve state consistency.

**DaemonSet** ensures one pod runs on every node (or a subset matching node selectors/affinity). Used for node-level agents: log collectors (Fluentd, Vector), monitoring agents (Datadog, Prometheus node-exporter), CSI drivers, network plugins, kube-proxy. As you add nodes, the DaemonSet automatically schedules a pod on each new one.

**Job** runs pods to completion (rather than restarting them indefinitely). For batch processing, data migrations, one-time setup tasks. **CronJob** is Job + cron schedule — runs jobs on a schedule (backups, scheduled reports).

A fifth often-mentioned primitive is **ReplicaSet**, but you almost never create one directly — Deployment manages ReplicaSets for you.

```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph D[Deployment - stateless] DDeploy[Deployment: web-api
replicas: 3] --> DRS[ReplicaSet] DRS --> DP1[Pod web-api-abc123] DRS --> DP2[Pod web-api-def456] DRS --> DP3[Pod web-api-ghi789] end subgraph S[StatefulSet - stable identity] SDeploy[StatefulSet: mysql
replicas: 3] --> SP0[Pod mysql-0

+ PVC mysql-data-1] SDeploy --> SP2[Pod mysql-2
+ PVC mysql-data-2] end subgraph DS[DaemonSet - one per node] DSDeploy[DaemonSet: fluentd] --> N1[Node 1: fluentd pod] DSDeploy --> N2[Node 2: fluentd pod] DSDeploy --> N3[Node 3: fluentd pod] end subgraph J[Job - run to completion] JDeploy[Job: db-migration] --> JP[Pod runs once] JP --> JDone[Completed; not restarted] end style D fill:#e3f2fd style S fill:#fff9c4 style DS fill:#fce4ec style J fill:#c8e6c9 ``` Deployment pods get random names; StatefulSet pods get ordinal names with persistent storage; DaemonSet schedules one per node; Job runs once.

sections.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Deployment | StatefulSet | DaemonSet | Job / CronJob |
|--------|------------|-------------|-----------|---------------|
| **Pod naming** | Random hash (web-abc123) | Ordinal (mysql-0, mysql-1) | One per node | random or templated |
| **Persistent storage** | Optional shared | Per-pod (volumeClaimTemplates) | Optional | Optional |
| **Network identity** | Random IPs, behind Service | Stable DNS via headless Service | Random | Random |
| **Rollout strategy** | Rolling (parallel) | Ordered (sequential) | Rolling | N/A (run once) |
| **Scale** | Horizontal, fast | Horizontal, slow (ordered) | Tied to node count | N/A |
| **Use case** | Stateless apps | Databases, distributed systems | Node-level agents | Batch, migrations |
| **Examples** | Web APIs, microservices | MySQL, Kafka, ZooKeeper, Elasticsearch | Fluentd, node-exporter, CSI drivers | DB migration, backups, batch jobs |
| **Termination** | Pods restart on failure | Pods restart with same identity | Removed when node removed | Job ends; pods removed (configurable) |
| **Common mistake** | Using for stateful workloads | Using when external DB suffices | Forgetting tolerations for tainted nodes | Running long-running services as Jobs |

sections.title: When to Pick Each (with Concrete Examples)
sections.content:
**Use Deployment for:**
- Stateless web APIs and microservices (Spring Boot service, Node.js API, Python Flask)
- Background workers consuming from a queue (where state is in the queue, not the worker)
- Frontend services (React/Next.js apps)
- Anything where adding/removing a replica has no consequence beyond load distribution

The canonical example: a payment-service Deployment with 5 replicas behind a Service. Each pod is interchangeable; load balancer distributes requests.

**Use StatefulSet for:**
- Databases that you self-host: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra
- Distributed systems with node identity: Kafka brokers, ZooKeeper, Elasticsearch nodes
- Any workload where pod-N specifically must always come back as pod-N with the same data

A Kafka StatefulSet creates broker-0, broker-1, broker-2 with stable DNS names (`broker-0.kafka.default.svc.cluster.local`) and persistent volumes. If broker-1 crashes and restarts, it comes back as broker-1 with its same volume.

**The most common StatefulSet mistake**: using one when the database is actually external (RDS, Aurora, managed Mongo). If your application connects to an external DB, the application is stateless from K8s's perspective — use a Deployment. StatefulSets are for when K8s is managing the stateful workload itself.

**Use DaemonSet for:**
- Log shipping: Fluentd, Vector, Filebeat collecting logs from each node
- Monitoring agents: Datadog Agent, Prometheus node-exporter
- Storage drivers: CSI drivers (Rook Ceph, Longhorn)
- Network plugins: Calico, Cilium, kube-proxy
- Anything that needs to run once per node to interact with node-local resources

DaemonSets respect node selectors and tolerations — you can run on all nodes, or only Linux nodes, or only nodes with GPUs.

**Use Job for:**
- Database migrations on deploy (Flyway/Liquibase Job that runs before app rollout)
- One-time data migrations
- Backup tasks (though CronJob is more common)
- Batch processing: data ETL, report generation

Use CronJob for:
- Scheduled backups (`kubectl get cronjob backup-db`)
- Periodic cleanup tasks
- Recurring report generation
- The K8s equivalent of crontab

sections.title: Hidden Trade-offs and Operational Pitfalls
sections.content:
**StatefulSet rollouts are slow.** Pods come up one at a time, in order, waiting for each to be Ready before starting the next. A 5-replica StatefulSet update takes 5x as long as a Deployment. For databases this is correct (you don't want all replicas restarting at once), but it means StatefulSet rollouts can take 10+ minutes.

**StatefulSet scale-down is intentional.** Decreasing replicas removes the highest-ordinal pod first, but its PVC is NOT automatically deleted (data preservation). If you scale back up, the new pod-N reattaches to the existing PVC with its data intact. This is great for safety but creates orphaned PVCs you must clean up manually.

**Headless service required for StatefulSet DNS.** A regular Service load-balances; for stable DNS per pod (`mysql-0.mysql.default.svc`), you need a headless Service (`clusterIP: None`). Forgetting this is the most common StatefulSet bug.

**Should you really self-host stateful systems on K8s?** The pendulum has swung. Operators (Cloudnative-PG, Strimzi for Kafka, Elasticsearch operator) make self-hosting more reliable. But for production at any scale, managed services (RDS, MSK, Elastic Cloud) eliminate operational burden. Pick StatefulSet when managed isn't an option (cost, regulatory, multi-cloud) or when you have a dedicated platform team.

**DaemonSet scaling pain.** Adding a node = adding all your DaemonSet pods. With 50 DaemonSets (logging, monitoring, storage, network), each new node spins up 50 pods. This burns memory and consumes IP addresses. Audit your DaemonSets periodically.

**Tolerations for tainted nodes.** DaemonSets don't run on tainted nodes by default. If you want logging on control-plane nodes, the DaemonSet needs `tolerations` for the control-plane taint. Common gotcha for new clusters.

**Job retention.** Completed Jobs and their pods stick around for inspection. Use `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` to auto-clean. Without this, finished pods accumulate and consume resources.

**CronJob concurrency policy.** Default is `Allow` — multiple invocations can run concurrently. If a backup takes longer than the schedule interval, you get overlapping runs. Set `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` or `Replace` based on intent.

**Job retries can hide failures.** `backoffLimit` controls retries before giving up. The default of 6 means a broken Job retries 6 times — if each retry takes 10 minutes, that's an hour of failure before alerting. Tune to your context.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Deployment** for stateless services — the 90% default; rolling updates; pods are interchangeable
- **StatefulSet** for stateful systems with stable identity — databases, Kafka, Cassandra; ordinal names, per-pod PVC, slow ordered rollouts
- **DaemonSet** for one pod per node — log shippers, monitoring agents, CSI drivers; scales with node count
- **Job/CronJob** for run-to-completion or scheduled tasks — migrations, backups, batch processing
- **Common mistake**: using StatefulSet when DB is external (RDS, managed Mongo); the app is stateless, use Deployment
- **Headless service required for StatefulSet DNS** — `clusterIP: None`; gives stable per-pod DNS like mysql-0.mysql.default.svc
- **CronJob concurrency policy matters** — default Allow can run overlapping if a job exceeds its interval; usually want Forbid or Replace

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Four Kubernetes workload primitives, each purpose-built for a specific operational pattern. Picking the wrong one leads to subtle pain.

**Deployment — the 90% default**
- For stateless services where pods are interchangeable: web APIs, microservices, background workers, frontends
- Manages ReplicaSets which manage Pods; rolling updates are the default; rollback via `kubectl rollout undo`
- Random pod names (web-abc123); pod can be killed and recreated anywhere with no consequence beyond load distribution

**StatefulSet — for systems that need stable identity**
- For databases (MySQL, Postgres, Mongo), distributed systems (Kafka, ZooKeeper, Cassandra, Elasticsearch)
- Pods get deterministic ordinal names (mysql-0, mysql-1, mysql-2) and stable DNS via a headless service
- Each pod gets its own PersistentVolumeClaim from volumeClaimTemplates; PVC follows the pod through rescheduling
- Rollouts are sequential — pods come up one at a time in order, waiting for each Ready before starting the next; safer for stateful systems but slower

**The most common StatefulSet mistake**
- Using one when the database is actually external (RDS, Aurora, managed Mongo)
- If your application connects to an external DB, the application is stateless from K8s's perspective — use a Deployment
- StatefulSets are only for when K8s is managing the stateful workload itself

**DaemonSet — one pod per node**
- For node-level agents: log collectors (Fluentd, Vector), monitoring agents (Datadog, Prometheus node-exporter), CSI drivers, network plugins like kube-proxy
- As you add nodes, the DaemonSet automatically schedules a pod on each new one
- Respects node selectors and tolerations — you can run on all nodes, only Linux nodes, only GPU nodes
- Common gotcha: DaemonSets don't run on tainted nodes by default; need explicit tolerations for control-plane nodes

**Job and CronJob — run to completion or on schedule**
- Job runs pods until they complete successfully (rather than restarting indefinitely)
- Use for database migrations on deploy, one-time data migrations, batch processing
- CronJob is Job plus a cron schedule — K8s equivalent of crontab; backups, scheduled reports
- Set `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` to auto-clean completed Job pods; without it they accumulate
- Set `concurrencyPolicy` on CronJobs — default Allow means overlapping runs if a job exceeds its interval; usually want Forbid or Replace

**The bigger question**
- Should you really self-host stateful systems on K8s? The pendulum has swung — operators (Cloudnative-PG, Strimzi for Kafka, Elasticsearch operator) make self-hosting more reliable
- But for production at scale, managed services (RDS, MSK, Elastic Cloud) eliminate operational burden
- Use StatefulSet when managed isn't an option (cost, regulatory, multi-cloud) or when you have a dedicated platform team

**Operational pitfalls to call out**
- StatefulSet scale-down doesn't delete PVCs (data preservation); orphaned PVCs accumulate and need cleanup
- DaemonSet scaling: adding a node spins up all your DaemonSet pods; with 50 DaemonSets that's 50 extra pods per new node
- Job retries can hide failures — default backoffLimit of 6 means a broken Job retries 6 times before giving up; tune for your context
